title: Integrating SQL, Spreadsheets, and pandas
summary: Apply already-learned SQL, spreadsheet, and pandas skills to the QuickRide capstone project: retrieve last quarter's orders with a multi-clause SELECT, summarise the delivery sheet with a PivotTable and COUNTIFS, clean and aggregate orders in pandas, and model the two-table relationship with correct primary and foreign keys.

steps.title: One SELECT statement: JOIN, WHERE, and GROUP BY together
steps.lede: The first step of the QuickRide capstone is retrieving last quarter's delivery data. All the SQL clauses you already know — JOIN, WHERE, and GROUP BY — can live in a single SELECT statement.

blocks.text: Combining clauses in one query

A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query. In the capstone, that means one statement can filter orders down to last quarter's rows **and** group the result by zone — no separate steps needed.

An INNER JOIN can be included in that same FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table **before** WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied. In the capstone, the `orders` and `drivers` tables are joined in the FROM clause first; the WHERE and GROUP BY then narrow and group the combined rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.zone,
       AVG(o.delivery_time) AS avg_delivery_time
FROM   orders o
       INNER JOIN drivers d
           ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id
WHERE  o.order_date >= '2026-04-01'
  AND  o.order_date <  '2026-07-01'
GROUP BY o.zone;

annotations.text: FROM + INNER JOIN: combines each order row with its matching driver row first.
WHERE: narrows the combined rows to last quarter (2026-04-01 to 2026-06-30).
GROUP BY: groups the filtered rows by zone so AVG gives one value per zone.

steps.title: Clause order: join first, filter next, group last
steps.lede: The capstone query uses the same SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY you already know — aimed at QuickRide's own tables and date range.

blocks.text: In the capstone query, the INNER JOIN in the FROM clause combines each order row with its matching driver row first. The WHERE clause then narrows those combined rows to orders placed between 2026-04-01 and 2026-06-30. Finally, GROUP BY groups what remains by zone, so AVG(delivery_time) returns one average per zone. None of this is new syntax — it is the same clauses already learned, applied to QuickRide's own tables.

steps.title: Where does the INNER JOIN go?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of where a JOIN fits inside a SELECT statement.

public.prompt: In a SELECT statement that also has a WHERE clause and a GROUP BY clause, where does an INNER JOIN appear?

options.text: In the FROM clause, before WHERE and GROUP BY are applied.
In the WHERE clause, alongside the filter conditions.
In the GROUP BY clause, to combine groups from both tables.
In the SELECT clause, to choose which columns to combine.

opt_from.message: Correct. The INNER JOIN is part of the FROM clause: it combines matching rows from both tables before the WHERE filter and GROUP BY grouping are applied.

opt_where.message: The WHERE clause filters rows after the tables have already been joined. The JOIN itself belongs in the FROM clause, not in WHERE.

opt_group.message: GROUP BY groups the already-joined and already-filtered rows into summary groups. The JOIN that combines the two tables happens earlier, in the FROM clause.

opt_select.message: SELECT names the columns to return from the result. The JOIN that combines rows from two tables is specified in the FROM clause, not in SELECT.

correct.message: Right. INNER JOIN ... ON goes inside the FROM clause, so the database combines the two tables first, then applies WHERE and GROUP BY.

incorrect.message: Think about the order SQL processes a query: it first assembles the rows (FROM + JOIN), then filters them (WHERE), then groups them (GROUP BY). Which clause assembles the rows?

hints: SQL processes FROM before WHERE and GROUP BY. The JOIN is part of assembling the rows, not filtering or grouping them.
The syntax is: FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id — notice it sits right after FROM.

steps.title: Write the capstone retrieval query
steps.lede: Write the SQL query that retrieves last quarter's QuickRide orders, joining the orders and drivers tables, filtering to the correct date range, and grouping by zone.

public.prompt:
Two tables are available: **orders** (columns: order_id, driver_id, zone, order_date, delivery_time) and **drivers** (columns: driver_id, driver_name).

The query below is almost complete. Add the GROUP BY clause at the end to group by zone.

The result should have one row per zone with the average delivery_time.

files.content:
SELECT zone, AVG(delivery_time)
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id
WHERE order_date >= '2026-04-01' AND order_date < '2026-07-01'
-- Add GROUP BY clause here

solution_files.content:
SELECT zone, AVG(delivery_time)
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id
WHERE order_date >= '2026-04-01' AND order_date < '2026-07-01'
GROUP BY zone

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return one row per zone with the average delivery_time for orders placed between 2026-04-01 and 2026-06-30. Check your JOIN condition, date filter, and GROUP BY clause.

correct.message: Well done. Your query joins the two tables, filters to last quarter, and groups by zone — all in one SELECT statement.

incorrect.message: Check that your query has INNER JOIN in the FROM clause, a WHERE clause with both date conditions joined by AND, and GROUP BY zone.

hints: The INNER JOIN goes right after the first table name in FROM: FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id.
The WHERE clause needs two conditions: o.order_date >= '2026-04-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-07-01'.

steps.title: PivotTable and COUNTIFS on the capstone delivery sheet
steps.lede: The capstone's spreadsheet step pairs each order's zone and delivery_time with the driver's shift. A PivotTable and COUNTIFS turn that sheet into a zone-by-shift summary.

blocks.text: Building a PivotTable from the delivery sheet

A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values. Fields can be dragged between areas to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, `zone` and `shift` (both non-numeric) default to Rows, while `delivery_time` (numeric) goes to Values.

COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]…) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells where **all** criteria are met. In the capstone, `COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45")` counts how many Ikeja deliveries exceeded 45 minutes.

annotations.text: PivotTable output: zone × shift grid, Average delivery_time per cell
COUNTIFS: counts rows where zone=Ikeja AND delivery_time>45

steps.title: Rearranging the PivotTable and applying COUNTIFS
steps.lede: Dragging shift from Rows to Columns turns the PivotTable into a zone-by-shift grid. COUNTIFS then counts deliveries that meet two criteria at once.

blocks.text: For the capstone delivery sheet, selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable places `zone` and `shift` in Rows by default and `delivery_time` in Values. Dragging `shift` from Rows to Columns rearranges the summary into a zone-by-shift grid; changing the Values summary function to Average makes each cell an average delivery time.

Separately, `COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45")` counts how many Ikeja deliveries in the sheet took more than 45 minutes — both criteria (zone and time threshold) must be met at once. The PivotTable and COUNTIFS skills already learned are now run on this project's own roster and delivery data.

steps.title: Applying COUNTIFS with multiple criteria
steps.lede: Test your understanding of how COUNTIFS handles more than one criterion.

public.prompt: A spreadsheet has zone values in column A and delivery_time values in column C (rows 2–37). Which formula correctly counts the rows where zone is 'Ikeja' AND delivery_time is greater than 45?

options.text: =COUNTIFS(A2:A37,"Ikeja",C2:C37,">45")
=COUNTIF(A2:A37,"Ikeja",C2:C37,">45")
=COUNTIFS(C2:C37,">45","Ikeja",A2:A37)
=SUMIF(A2:A37,"Ikeja",C2:C37)

opt_correct.message: Correct. COUNTIFS takes pairs of (criteria_range, criteria): the first pair checks zone = 'Ikeja' and the second checks delivery_time > 45. Both criteria must be met for a row to be counted.

opt_countif_single.message: COUNTIF (without the S) accepts only one criteria range and one criterion. To apply two criteria at once you need COUNTIFS, which takes pairs of (range, criterion) and counts rows where all criteria are met.

opt_wrong_order.message: COUNTIFS expects each criterion immediately after its range: (range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2). Placing the criterion text 'Ikeja' where a range is expected causes an error.

opt_sumif.message: SUMIF adds up values in a sum range where a single criterion is met — it does not count rows. To count rows matching multiple criteria, use COUNTIFS.

correct.message: Exactly right. COUNTIFS(range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2) counts rows where every criterion is satisfied.

incorrect.message: COUNTIFS takes pairs of (criteria_range, criteria). Make sure you are using COUNTIFS (not COUNTIF) and that each range is immediately followed by its criterion.

hints: COUNTIF handles one criterion; COUNTIFS handles one or more. Here you have two criteria, so you need COUNTIFS.
The syntax is COUNTIFS(range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2). Each range must come right before its matching criterion.

opt_pivot_countifs.message: Correct. A PivotTable with zone in Rows, shift in Columns, and average delivery_time in Values produces the zone-by-shift grid. A separate COUNTIFS formula counts rows matching both the zone and the delivery_time threshold.

opt_pivot_only.message: A PivotTable can produce the zone-by-shift average grid, but it cannot directly apply a threshold filter like 'delivery_time > 45' to count matching rows. That requires a COUNTIFS formula.

opt_sumif_pivot.message: SUMIF adds values matching one criterion — it does not produce a two-dimensional average grid. The grid needs a PivotTable, and the filtered count needs COUNTIFS.

incorrect.message: Think about what each tool does: a PivotTable creates a cross-tabulation of averages; COUNTIFS counts rows matching multiple criteria. Which task needs which tool?

hints: A PivotTable can cross-tabulate averages by two categorical fields (zone and shift). Can it also apply a numeric threshold filter to count rows?
COUNTIFS(range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2) counts rows where all criteria are met — it does not produce a grid of averages.

steps.title: Cleaning and grouping the capstone orders in pandas
steps.lede: Once orders are retrieved, pandas handles cleaning and aggregation. isna()/dropna() remove missing delivery times; groupby().mean() produces one average per zone.

blocks.text: Detecting and removing missing values

isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values — or fillna() replaces them with a specified value. In the capstone, `orders['delivery_time'].isna()` flags rows with no delivery time recorded; those rows are then removed with dropna() before any aggregation.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure. An aggregation reduces each group to one summary value per column. In the capstone, `orders.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()` splits the cleaned orders by zone and returns one mean delivery time per zone.

before.caption: Raw orders DataFrame — NaN delivery_time rows visible

result_of.sql: SELECT zone, AVG(delivery_time) AS mean_delivery_time FROM ds_pandas_orders WHERE delivery_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY zone ORDER BY zone

after.caption: After dropna() + groupby('zone').mean() — one mean per zone

blocks.change_summary: dropna() removes rows where delivery_time is NULL; groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() reduces each zone to one average.

steps.title: The same skills, applied to the capstone's own data
steps.lede: The isna()/dropna()/fillna() and groupby() skills already learned are now run on the capstone's retrieved orders instead of a practice dataset.

blocks.text: On the capstone's retrieved orders, `orders['delivery_time'].isna()` flags rows with no delivery time; dropna() removes them. Then `orders.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()` splits the cleaned orders by zone, computes the mean delivery time within each zone, and combines the per-zone results — an aggregation, since each zone group is reduced to a single number.

steps.title: Cleaning and aggregating the capstone dataset end-to-end
steps.lede: Test your understanding of how isna()/dropna() and groupby().mean() work together to clean and summarise the capstone orders.

public.prompt: A DataFrame `df` has columns `zone` and `delivery_time`, with some NaN values in `delivery_time`. Which sequence of operations produces a Series showing the mean delivery_time per zone, using only rows where delivery_time is not missing?

options.text: df.dropna() then df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()
df.fillna(0) then df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()
df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() directly, without any cleaning step
df.isna() then df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()

opt_correct.message: Correct. dropna() removes rows with any NaN value, so the subsequent groupby().mean() computes the mean only from rows with a recorded delivery_time.

opt_fillna_group.message: fillna(0) replaces NaN with 0, which pulls the mean downward — a 0-minute delivery is not a real observation. To exclude missing rows entirely, use dropna() instead.

opt_group_only.message: pandas groupby().mean() skips NaN values by default, so the result would be numerically the same. However, calling dropna() first makes the cleaning step explicit in your code: anyone reading the workflow can see that missing rows were intentionally removed, making the analysis visible and reproducible rather than relying on a silent default.

opt_isna_group.message: isna() returns a boolean DataFrame showing where values are missing — it does not remove those rows. To remove rows with missing values, use dropna().

correct.message: Right. dropna() removes rows with missing delivery_time, then groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() computes one mean per zone.

incorrect.message: Think about what each method does: isna() detects missing values, dropna() removes rows with them, fillna() replaces them. Which one removes the rows so the mean is computed only from real observations?

hints: isna() returns True/False for each cell — it does not change the DataFrame. dropna() actually removes rows that contain NaN.
fillna(0) keeps all rows but replaces NaN with 0. Would a 0-minute delivery time give a correct mean?

steps.title: Detect missing values and compute per-zone means
steps.lede: Given a small orders DataFrame with zone and delivery_time columns (some NaN), detect the missing delivery times, remove those rows, then compute the mean delivery time per zone.

public.prompt:
The DataFrame `df` is loaded from `orders.csv` with columns `zone` and `delivery_time`. Some `delivery_time` values are NaN.

1. Print the result of `df['delivery_time'].isna()` to see which rows are missing.
2. Remove rows with missing delivery_time using `dropna()` and reassign the result to `df`.
3. Compute the mean delivery_time per zone using `groupby` and `mean()`. Assign the result to a variable named `zone_means` and print it.

The final output must show one mean delivery_time value per zone.

files.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# Step 1: print which delivery_time values are missing
# print(df['delivery_time'].isna())

# Step 2: remove rows with missing delivery_time
# df = df.dropna()

# Step 3: compute mean delivery_time per zone and print

solution_files.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# Step 1: print which delivery_time values are missing
print(df['delivery_time'].isna())

# Step 2: remove rows with missing delivery_time
df = df.dropna()

# Step 3: compute mean delivery_time per zone and print
zone_means = df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()
print(zone_means)

incorrect.message: Make sure you: (1) call df.dropna() and reassign the result to 'df', and (2) call df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() to get one mean per zone.

To get one mean per zone: df.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean()

steps.title: Primary keys, foreign keys, and one-to-many in the capstone
steps.lede: The capstone spans two tables — Orders and Drivers. Before any join or aggregation across them can be trusted, the key columns and their relationship need to be correctly identified.

blocks.text: Primary keys and foreign keys

A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references. In the capstone, the Drivers table needs a column that uniquely identifies each driver, and the Orders table needs a column whose values must match one of those driver identifiers.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side — for example, one department has many employees. In the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table. In the capstone, one driver can appear in many orders: the same one-to-many pattern.

blocks.title: Capstone data model: Drivers (1) → Orders (many)
blocks.alt_text: Entity-relationship diagram showing two boxes: Drivers (driver_id as PK, driver_name) and Orders (order_id as PK, driver_id as FK, zone, order_date, delivery_time). An arrow from Drivers.driver_id to Orders.driver_id is labelled '1:N — one driver → many orders'.

steps.title: Mapping the capstone tables onto the model
steps.lede: Getting the primary key / foreign key pairing right connects the two tables correctly before any join or aggregation across them can be trusted.

blocks.text: In the capstone: Drivers has `driver_id` as its primary key, uniquely identifying each driver row. Orders has its own primary key, `order_id`, plus a `driver_id` column that is a foreign key — its values must match a `driver_id` that already exists in Drivers. Since one driver delivers many orders, this is a one-to-many relationship: one row on the Drivers ('one') side relates to many rows on the Orders ('many') side.

steps.title: Identifying the one-to-many relationship in the capstone
steps.lede: Test your understanding of the one-to-many relationship between the Drivers and Orders tables.

public.prompt: In the capstone data model, one driver can deliver many orders, but each order is assigned to exactly one driver. Which statement correctly describes this relationship?

options.text: Drivers is on the 'one' side and Orders is on the 'many' side; the foreign key driver_id is placed in the Orders table.
Orders is on the 'one' side and Drivers is on the 'many' side; the foreign key is placed in the Drivers table.
It is a many-to-many relationship because a driver can have many orders and an order can have many drivers.
It is a one-to-one relationship because each order has exactly one driver.

opt_one_to_many.message: Correct. Drivers is on the 'one' side (one driver) and Orders is on the 'many' side (many orders per driver). The foreign key driver_id is placed in the Orders table and must match a valid driver_id in the Drivers table.

opt_many_to_one.message: The sides are reversed. Drivers is on the 'one' side because one driver can have many orders. The foreign key goes in the 'many' table — Orders — not in Drivers.

opt_many_to_many.message: Each order is assigned to exactly one driver, so the relationship is not many-to-many. One driver can have many orders, but each order has only one driver — that is a one-to-many relationship.

opt_one_to_one.message: One-to-one means each row on one side matches exactly one row on the other. Here, one driver can match many orders, so the relationship is one-to-many, not one-to-one.

correct.message: Right. One driver → many orders. The foreign key driver_id lives in the Orders table and references the Drivers table.

incorrect.message: Ask: can one driver have more than one order? Yes — so Drivers is on the 'one' side and Orders is on the 'many' side. The foreign key goes in the 'many' table.

hints: The 'one' side is the table where each row can relate to multiple rows in the other table. Which table is that here — Drivers or Orders?
In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key is always placed in the 'many' table to reference the 'one' table.

remediation_steps.title: Where does the INNER JOIN go in a SELECT statement?
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked where an INNER JOIN fits inside a SELECT. Here's the key rule.

blocks.text: An INNER JOIN is placed in the **FROM clause** of a SELECT statement — not in WHERE or GROUP BY. The FROM clause (including any JOINs) runs first, combining matching rows from both tables. The WHERE clause then filters those combined rows, and GROUP BY groups what remains. In the capstone query, `FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id` combines the two tables before any filtering or grouping.

A common mistake is placing the JOIN condition in the WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE o.driver_id = d.driver_id`). While some databases accept this older syntax, the standard and clearer approach is `INNER JOIN … ON` in the FROM clause, which makes the join explicit and keeps the WHERE clause for row filtering only.

remediation_steps.title: How COUNTIFS applies multiple criteria
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked how COUNTIFS handles more than one criterion. Here's the key rule.

blocks.text: COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2) counts only the rows where **all** criteria are met simultaneously. Each criteria_range/criteria pair is evaluated independently, and only rows that pass every pair are counted. In the capstone, `COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45")` counts rows where the zone is Ikeja **and** the delivery time exceeds 45 minutes — both conditions must hold.

COUNTIFS is not the same as two separate COUNTIF calls added together. Adding two COUNTIF results would count rows that meet either criterion, not both. COUNTIFS enforces all criteria at once, so the count is always ≤ the count from any single criterion alone.

remediation_steps.title: PivotTable field placement and COUNTIFS together
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about executing the full capstone spreadsheet analysis step. Here are the two key rules.

blocks.text: When you add a field to a PivotTable, the tool places it based on its data type: **non-numeric fields** (like zone and shift) default to Rows, **date/time fields** default to Columns, and **numeric fields** (like delivery_time) default to Values. You can drag any field between Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, dragging `shift` from Rows to Columns turns the layout into a zone-by-shift grid.

remediation_steps.title: Cleaning and aggregating: isna()/dropna() then groupby().mean()
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about the full clean-and-aggregate workflow. Here are the two steps.

blocks.text: isna() returns a boolean mask showing which values are missing (NaN). dropna() removes rows with missing values; fillna(value) replaces them. In the capstone, `orders["delivery_time"].isna()` identifies which orders have no recorded delivery time; dropna() removes those rows before any aggregation runs.

A groupby operation splits data into groups, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results. An aggregation reduces each group to one summary value. In the capstone, `orders.groupby("zone")["delivery_time"].mean()` splits the cleaned orders by zone and returns one mean delivery time per zone — an aggregation.

remediation_steps.title: The one-to-many relationship between Drivers and Orders
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked about the one-to-many relationship in the capstone. Here is the key rule.

blocks.text: In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the "one" side relates to many rows on the "many" side. The foreign key is placed on the "many" side. In the capstone, one driver (Drivers table, "one" side) can appear in many orders (Orders table, "many" side), so `driver_id` as a foreign key sits in the Orders table — the same pattern as CustID sitting in the Order table.

A common mistake is placing the foreign key on the "one" side. The foreign key always goes on the "many" side — the table that can have multiple rows for the same related entity. In the capstone, Orders (many orders per driver) holds the `driver_id` foreign key, not Drivers.
